## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Describe** **multi-head attention** (each head projects the whole token to its own smaller
  queries, keys and values; attend in each; concatenate; mix), state its cost correctly, and **test with
  an ablation** what each trained head contributes. *(Understand / Analyze)*
- **Explain** **positional encoding**: why self-attention without a causal mask is blind to order,

## Why This Matters

L21 ended with two sentences made of the same words:

> "this movie is not bad, it is good"
>
> "this movie is not good, it is bad"

Its attention classifier gave both the same probability of being positive, 0.8448, to four decimals.
Self-attention compares words by content only, so shuffling the words only shuffles its outputs
(**equivariance**), and a readout that pools them cannot tell the two orders apart (**invariance**).

In 2017, Vaswani et al. showed that attention alone, with a few parts around it, could beat the best
translation models of the day. Their architecture, the **Transformer**, is now the core of BERT, GPT and
essentially every large language model. The parts are few:

- several attention computations side by side (**multi-head attention**);
- a signal that tells each token where it sits (**positional encoding**);
- a residual connection and a **layer normalization** around every sublayer, plus a small per-position
  network, packed into a **block** that can be stacked;
- for generating text, a **causal mask** that hides the future.

Each one fixes a specific problem, and the lab measures what each one changes.

## Multi-Head Attention

One attention layer gives each position **one** set of weights over the others, so it builds one
weighted blend per query. A sentence has several relations at once: which noun a pronoun refers to,
which verb goes with which subject, where a clause ends. **Multi-head attention** runs several
attentions in parallel, side by side. Each **head** $i$ projects the **whole** token, all $d$ numbers,
down to its own queries, keys and values of $d/h$ numbers, with its own matrices $W_q^i$, $W_k^i$,
$W_v^i$ of size $d \times d/h$; it runs scaled dot-product attention (L21) on them; the $h$ results are
concatenated back to width $d$ and mixed by a final matrix $W_o$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{head}_i &= \text{attention}(X W_q^i,\ X W_k^i,\ X W_v^i) \\
\text{MultiHead}(X) &= \operatorname{concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, W_o
\end{aligned}
$$

In the lab, $d = 64$ and $h = 4$: each head's matrices are $64 \times 16$. In code, the four heads'
$W_q^i$ sit side by side in one $64 \times 64$ matrix: project once, then cut the result into four
slices of 16. Inside a head, the scores are divided by $\sqrt{d/h} = \sqrt{16} = 4$, not by
$\sqrt{64}$.

Each head has its own projections, and all of them are trained together. On the lab's order task
("does marker A come before marker B?"), the classifier reads its answer from a `CLS` token at the
first position. Averaged over the 1,000 test sequences, one head of the `CLS` token in the last block
puts 0.998 of its weight on A and another puts 0.972 on B (@fig-heads shows one sequence). It looks like a clean
division of labor, but the weights only show where a head looks. The lab tests it by switching heads
off (an **ablation**): without the "B head" the model still scores 1.0000. Removing a third head, whose
A and B averages looked mixed, costs the most (0.9420), and that head alone is enough: sequence by
sequence, it looks at whichever marker comes **first** (0.791 of its weight on average), exactly what
the label asks. The heads overlap, and with other random starts the whole last block's attention can be
switched off at almost no cost, sharp heads and all. Attention weights are a hint, not an explanation
(L21); an ablation tests what a part contributes.

![Multi-head attention. Top: the whole token ($d = 64$) is projected by $W_q$, $W_k$, $W_v$ and the result cut into four heads of 16 numbers; each head attends on its own, and the four results are concatenated and mixed by $W_o$. Bottom: the trained order model's `CLS` attention in its last block, one row per head, for one test sequence. Head 0 looks at A, heads 1 and 3 at B; where a head looks is not the same as what the answer needs from it (the lab's ablation).](../assets/l22_heads.svg){#fig-heads width="100%" fig-alt="Top: a gray matrix X of L tokens by 64 features is projected by W q, W k, W v and cut into four colored slices of 16 features, head 0 to head 3; each slice goes through its own attention box giving an L by 16 result; the four results are concatenated into an L by 64 matrix, which is multiplied by W o to give the output, L by 64. Bottom: four rows of twelve cells with attention weights, one row per head, over the tokens of test sequence 0 (CLS, B, 7, 6, 6, A, 3, 8, 3, 6, 7, 9; B comes before A, label 0). Head 0 puts weight 1.00 on A, heads 1 and 3 put 1.00 on B, and head 2 spreads its weight, 0.45 of it on CLS."}

**Cost.** The four heads' matrix products (the projections, the scores $QK^\top$, and the blend of the
values) add up to the same arithmetic as one head over all 64 numbers. The softmax does not: it runs
over $h$ score matrices of $L \times L$ instead of one. Nor does the memory, in an implementation that
stores the weights, like the lab's: every head keeps its own $L \times L$ weight matrix. For one sequence
of 1,024 tokens the lab measures 4 MB of weights with one head and 16 MB with four, L21's quadratic
memory multiplied by $h$. Fused kernels such as FlashAttention (L21) compute the same result in tiles
and never store the full matrices, though the arithmetic still grows with $L^2$. PyTorch ships the layer
as `nn.MultiheadAttention`; the lab checks that the class you build gives the same output to within
$10^{-6}$.

## Positional Encoding

Self-attention without a causal mask sees a set. To give it order, **add** a position vector $p_t$ to the vector of the token at
position $t$, before the first block, so that the same word at two places becomes two different vectors.
The original Transformer uses a fixed **sinusoidal** encoding. For each pair of dimensions $(2i, 2i+1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
PE_{(t,\,2i)} &= \sin\!\left(t / 10000^{\,2i/d}\right) \\
PE_{(t,\,2i+1)} &= \cos\!\left(t / 10000^{\,2i/d}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

By hand with $d = 4$: the first pair ($i = 0$) uses $t / 1$ and the second pair ($i = 1$) uses
$t / 10000^{2/4} = t / 100$, so

| Position $t$ | $\sin(t)$ | $\cos(t)$ | $\sin(t/100)$ | $\cos(t/100)$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 0.841 | 0.540 | 0.010 | 1.000 |
| 2 | 0.909 | -0.416 | 0.020 | 1.000 |

The first pair turns fast and separates neighbors; the second turns slowly and separates positions far
apart. With 64 dimensions the frequencies range over many scales, and every position gets its own
pattern (@fig-positions, left). A side effect: the dot product of two position vectors depends only on
their **offset**, not on where they sit. It is largest at offset 0 and, over short distances, falls
off with some ripples (@fig-positions, right). Two limits keep this from being a ready-made sense of
relative position. The dot product is **symmetric**, so it cannot tell "before" from "after". And it
does not keep falling: with $d = 64$ it is 22.4 at offset 8 and 19.4 at offset 16, but 19.6 at offset
32, and 11.3 at offset 256 against 9.1 at 128. Besides, attention compares *projected* vectors
($W_q$ and $W_k$ sit in between), so a model has to learn what to do with position; this property is
not handed to it.

![Sinusoidal positional encoding, $d = 64$. Left: the encoding for positions 0 to 15, one column per position; low dimensions change fast, high dimensions slowly. Right: the dot product of the encoding of position 32 with every position from 0 to 63; over this range it peaks at 32 and, with ripples, falls off on both sides, the same way at every starting position. At larger offsets it oscillates rather than keep falling.](../assets/l22_positions.svg){#fig-positions width="100%" fig-alt="Left: a heat map, positions 0 to 15 on the horizontal axis and encoding dimensions 0 to 63 on the vertical axis, red for plus 1 and blue for minus 1; the bottom rows alternate quickly between red and blue, the top rows are nearly constant. Right: a line chart of the dot product with position 32 against positions 0 to 63, symmetric around a sharp peak of 32 at position 32, dropping quickly and then wavering at a lower level."}

**Why add rather than append?** Adding keeps the width $d$ unchanged, and the network can learn to keep
word information and position information in different directions of the same vector.

Two other encodings matter in practice:

- **Learned positions:** a trainable table `nn.Embedding(max_len, d)`, looked up by position exactly like
  a token embedding. BERT, GPT-2 and GPT-3 use it. The lab's Exercise 1 shows it solves the order task as
  well as the sinusoidal one.
- **Rotary position encoding (RoPE**, Su et al., 2021): it adds nothing to the token. Instead, inside
  **every** attention layer, it rotates each query and key by an angle that grows with its position,
  so the score between two tokens depends on their **signed offset** $t - s$: which one comes first,
  and by how much. LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen and most open language models released since 2023 use it.
  Named here, not built.

Whatever the form, the point is the same for self-attention **without a causal mask**, as in an
encoder: it treats its input as a set, no amount of depth can recover order from a set, so position has
to be put in. In the lab, the same small Transformer scores **about 0.48** (0.4810 in the committed run)
on the order task without positional encoding (always answering "A first" would score 0.517) and
**1.0000** with it. A decoder is different, and the section on causal masking comes back to it.

## Layer Normalization

A deep stack is easier to train when every sublayer receives inputs of a steady size. **Layer
normalization** standardizes each token **across its own features**: subtract the token's mean, divide by
its standard deviation, then apply a learned scale $\gamma$ and shift $\beta$ per feature (they start at
1 and 0):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{LN}(x) &= \gamma \odot \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta \\
\mu &= \tfrac{1}{d}\textstyle\sum_j x_j \\
\sigma^2 &= \tfrac{1}{d}\textstyle\sum_j (x_j - \mu)^2
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\epsilon$ (PyTorch: $10^{-5}$) only guards against dividing by zero.

**By hand**, for one token with four features, $x = (2, 4, 6, 8)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu &= (2 + 4 + 6 + 8) / 4 = 5 \\
\sigma^2 &= (9 + 1 + 1 + 9) / 4 = 5, \quad \sigma = 2.236 \\
\operatorname{LN}(x) &= (-3, -1, 1, 3) / 2.236 = (-1.342,\ -0.447,\ 0.447,\ 1.342)
\end{aligned}
$$

Before $\gamma$ and $\beta$, the result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (up to the tiny
$\epsilon$) whatever the token's original scale; the lab's Step 3 gets the same four numbers from
`nn.LayerNorm`. Training then adjusts $\gamma$ and $\beta$ per feature, so a trained layer norm's output
can have any mean and spread the model finds useful: what it removes is the token's own scale.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Your turn (by hand): two more tokens

Normalize (a) $x = (0, 3, 3, 6)$ and (b) $x = (5, 5, 5, 5)$, with $\gamma = 1$, $\beta = 0$. What does
$\epsilon$ do in (b)?

**Answer.** (a) $\mu = 3$, deviations $(-3, 0, 0, 3)$, $\sigma^2 = 18/4 = 4.5$, $\sigma = 2.121$, so
$\operatorname{LN}(x) = (-1.414,\ 0,\ 0,\ 1.414)$. (b) $\mu = 5$ and every deviation is 0, so
$\sigma^2 = 0$: without $\epsilon$ the formula would divide 0 by 0. With it, the result is
$(0, 0, 0, 0)$: a token with no variation carries no signal to standardize.
:::

**Layer norm is not batch norm.** L17's batch normalization standardizes each **feature across the
batch**, so a token's result depends on the other sequences in the batch, and the layer needs running
averages for test time. Layer norm uses one token's own numbers, so it gives the same answer alone, in
any batch, at training and at test time (the lab checks the batch half). For sequences of different lengths in
batches of any size, that is what Transformers need.

## The Transformer Block: Add & Norm

A Transformer is a stack of **blocks**, all with the same design and each with its own weights. Each
block has two **sublayers**:

- **multi-head self-attention**, which mixes information **between** positions;
- a **position-wise feed-forward network** (FFN), a two-layer MLP applied to each position on its own,
  usually 4 times wider in the middle (the lab: 64 to 128 to 64), which mixes the features **within**
  each position.

The FFN is the MLP of L14, applied to every token vector $x$ separately:

$$
\operatorname{FFN}(x) = \operatorname{ReLU}(x W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2
$$

with the same $W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2$ for every position of a block, and different ones in each block.

Each sublayer is wrapped the same way: a **residual connection** (L19: add the sublayer's input to its
output, so it only has to learn a change and gradients have a short path back) and a **layer norm**. The
2017 paper puts the norm after the addition, **Post-LN**; GPT-2 and most later models put it before the
sublayer, **Pre-LN** (@fig-block):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Post-LN:}\quad x &\leftarrow \operatorname{LN}\big(x + \text{sublayer}(x)\big) \\
\text{Pre-LN:}\quad x &\leftarrow x + \text{sublayer}\big(\operatorname{LN}(x)\big)
\end{aligned}
$$

![One encoder block, two ways. Post-LN (2017): each sublayer's output is added to its input and the sum is normalized. Pre-LN (GPT-2 and later): each sublayer sees a normalized copy of the input, and its output is added to the unnormalized input, so a clean residual path runs from the bottom of the stack to the top.](../assets/l22_block_post_pre.svg){#fig-block width="100%" fig-alt="Two block diagrams side by side, read from bottom to top. Left, Post-LN: input x goes into multi-head self-attention; a residual arrow skips around it to a plus node; the sum goes into a layer norm; then the same pattern with the feed-forward network: residual skip, plus, layer norm, output. Right, Pre-LN: input x goes into a layer norm and then multi-head self-attention, while a straight residual line carries x to a plus node; then layer norm, feed-forward network and a second plus node on the same straight line; output. The straight residual line on the right is highlighted."}

One consequence of Pre-LN: the main residual path is never normalized inside the stack, so its scale
can drift from block to block. Pre-LN models therefore add one last layer norm after the final block,
before the output layer (GPT-2 does; so does the lab's tiny GPT).

A block maps a sequence to a sequence of the same shape, so blocks stack. Follow one batch of $B$
sequences of $L$ tokens through a block with the lab's sizes ($d = 64$, four heads, FFN width 128):

| Step | Shape |
|---|---|
| token ids | `(B, L)` |
| token vectors + position signal | `(B, L, 64)` |
| queries, keys, values (one projection each) | `(B, L, 64)` |
| cut into four heads | `(B, 4, L, 16)` |
| scores and weights, one matrix per head | `(B, 4, L, L)` |
| weighted values, per head | `(B, 4, L, 16)` |
| heads concatenated, mixed by $W_o$, Add & Norm | `(B, L, 64)` |
| FFN hidden layer | `(B, L, 128)` |
| FFN output, Add & Norm: the block's output | `(B, L, 64)` |

Only two steps leave the `(B, L, 64)` shape: the heads (and their `L x L` weights) inside attention,
and the wider hidden layer inside the FFN. At $d = 64$ with four heads and an FFN width of 128, one
block has 33,472 parameters: 16,640 in the attention projections, 16,576 in the FFN and 256 in the two
layer norms. PyTorch's `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` is this block (`norm_first=True` gives Pre-LN); the
lab checks that its output matches ours exactly once dropout, which PyTorch's layer applies by default
during training, is switched off.

**What the residual and the norm's position do.** The lab trains the order task at two depths:

| Blocks | Variant | Test accuracy |
|---:|---|---:|
| 6 | Post-LN + residual | 1.0000 |
| 6 | Post-LN, **no residual** | 0.4830 |
| 12 | Post-LN + residual | 0.4830 |
| 12 | **Pre-LN** + residual | 1.0000 |

The two failures score exactly the share of label 0 in the test set: they answer 0 for every sequence
and never get started. Without the residual, the signal and the gradient must pass through every
freshly initialized sublayer in a row; with it, each block has a direct path around it. At 12 blocks,
the residual alone is not enough for Post-LN (stuck in two of three seeds in our tests), while Pre-LN
trained in every run. Post-LN is not broken: the 2017 paper trained it with a **learning-rate
warm-up** (start with tiny steps, grow them over the first part of training), and in the lab's
Exercise 2 a 60-step warm-up rescues the 12-block model (1.0000). Normalization's own job is to keep each
sublayer's input at a steady scale; in our tests this small task also trained with the residuals and no
normalization at all, so we claim no more for it here.

## Encoder, Decoder, Encoder-Decoder

Stack $N$ blocks and you have an **encoder**: every position gathers context from the whole sequence, $N$
times over. The same block, arranged differently, gives the three layouts you will meet (@fig-layouts):

- **Encoder-only:** every position sees every other: **no causal mask** (a padding mask still hides
  the padding when sequences of different lengths share a batch, as in L21 and the lab's IMDB
  classifier). It produces a representation of the whole input; a task head on top classifies, tags or
  retrieves. BERT is one; so is the lab's IMDB classifier.
- **Decoder-only:** the same block, with a **causal mask** (next section) on its self-attention, so
  each position sees only itself and earlier positions. It generates text left to right. GPT is one; so
  is the lab's tiny GPT, built from the lab's encoder block class plus the mask.
- **Encoder-decoder:** the original 2017 design for translation. The encoder reads the source sentence;
  the decoder writes the translation and, in each block, adds **cross-attention**: its queries come from
  the decoder, its keys and values from the encoder's output, so every word being written can look at
  the whole source sentence. (Explained here; the lab builds no encoder-decoder.)

![Three ways to arrange the same block. Encoder-only (BERT): no causal mask, every token sees every token. Decoder-only (GPT): a causal mask, each token sees only the past. Encoder-decoder (the 2017 translation model): an encoder over the source, and a decoder with causal self-attention plus cross-attention to the encoder's output.](../assets/l22_layouts.svg){#fig-layouts width="100%" fig-alt="Three panels. Left, encoder-only: a stack of N blocks labelled self-attention, no causal mask, over input tokens; a task head on top gives a class or tags; small grid icon fully shaded. Middle, decoder-only: a stack of N blocks labelled causal self-attention over tokens so far; the output is the next token; grid icon shaded only on and below the diagonal. Right, encoder-decoder: an encoder stack over the source sentence on the left; a decoder stack on the right whose blocks contain causal self-attention and cross-attention; an arrow from the top of the encoder enters every decoder block's cross-attention; the decoder outputs the next target word."}

## Causal Masking and Generation

An **autoregressive** (GPT-style) language model is trained to predict the **next** token at every
position (BERT is trained differently; see the next section). If position $t$ could see position
$t + 1$, it would just copy the answer. The **causal mask** forbids it: before the softmax, every
score above the diagonal (query $t$, key $s > t$) becomes $-\infty$, so its weight is exactly 0 and each
row's weights, over the positions it may see, still sum to 1. It is the padding mask of L21 with a
different pattern: in both, the mask says which keys a query **may** attend to, and the forbidden ones get
$-\infty$.

**Inputs, targets and the output layer.** The targets are the inputs shifted by one position. For the
text "the cat", read one character at a time:

~~~text
input    t  h  e  _  c  a
target   h  e  _  c  a  t
~~~

(`_` marks the space.) The last block gives one vector per position, a matrix $H$ of $L \times d$. A
linear **output layer** turns it into one score per vocabulary entry at every position, a softmax turns
each row into probabilities, and the loss is the cross-entropy of the true next token $y_t$, averaged
over the $L$ positions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z &= H\, W_{\text{vocab}} + b \qquad (L \times |V|) \\
P_t &= \operatorname{softmax}(Z_t) \\
\text{loss} &= -\tfrac{1}{L}\textstyle\sum_t \log P_{t,\,y_t}
\end{aligned}
$$

In the lab $|V| = 43$ characters, and one window of 64 characters gives 64 next-character examples at
once, each seeing exactly its own past: the mask is what makes training this efficient.

Generation then runs a loop (@fig-generation): feed the text so far, take the scores for the last
position, turn them into probabilities, **sample** the next token, append it, repeat. Dividing the
scores by a **temperature** before the softmax sharpens the distribution (below 1, more predictable and
more repetitive text) or flattens it (above 1, more varied and more errors). Training and generation
use the same model in different ways:

| | Training | Generation |
|---|---|---|
| Input | a known window of text | the prompt plus everything generated so far |
| Forward passes | one per window, all positions at once | one per new token, re-reading the context |
| Target | the known next token at every position | none: the next token does not exist yet |
| Scores used | at every position, for the loss | at the last position, to sample |
| Weights | updated by backpropagation | fixed |

Two practical details. The model has a fixed **context window** (64 characters in the lab), so a long
generation feeds it only the most recent 64. And recomputing every earlier position at every step is
wasteful: real systems keep each layer's past keys and values in memory, a **KV cache**, and compute
only the new position (named here, not built).

![Left: the causal mask for six positions; a query may attend to keys on and below the diagonal (shaded), never above it ($-\infty$). Right: generation, one character at a time: the model reads the text so far, predicts a distribution for the next character, one character is sampled and appended, and the longer text goes back in.](../assets/l22_causal_generation.svg){#fig-generation width="100%" fig-alt="Left: a 6 by 6 grid, rows labelled query 0 to 5 and columns key 0 to 5; cells on and below the diagonal are shaded blue, cells above the diagonal are white and marked minus infinity; a note reads shaded: may attend, minus infinity: weight 0. Right: a loop. A box 'text so far: this movie was' goes into a box 'tiny GPT (causal mask)'; an arrow labelled last position goes down to a box 'scores for the next character, divided by temperature, softmax'; an arrow goes to a box 'sample one character'; an arrow labelled append it, repeat leads back to the text box."}

The lab trains a tiny GPT (about 813,000 parameters, four Pre-LN blocks) on 5 million characters of IMDB
reviews for about 20 seconds on a T4 GPU. With the causal mask it reaches a validation loss of 1.544 (a uniform
guess over the 43 characters scores 3.761) and writes text like

> "this movie was a movie, but i hanted, a luche manet and to people ending it was ever to do get
> enough."

which is not English, but has English words, spacing and punctuation, learned from characters alone.
Trained **without** the mask, the same model reaches a loss of 0.035: it reads each answer one position
ahead. Measured with the future hidden, as in generation, its loss is about 6.6, worse than a uniform
guess, and it writes "this movie was sizhvsvssssssss...". Without the mask, the model learns to copy
the next character and nothing else.

**Does the tiny GPT use order?** Give it 64 characters and score its guess of the next one. With all
64 shuffled (the same characters, in a random order), its loss jumps from about 1.58 to about 4.9,
worse than a uniform guess; with the first 56 shuffled and the last 8 in place, it barely moves (about
1.59). It uses order, mostly the order of the last few characters.

**Does a decoder need a position signal?** Not the way an encoder does. With a causal mask, the input
is no longer a set: position 0 sees one token, position 1 sees two, position $t$ sees exactly $t + 1$,
so the model can work out where it is from what it is allowed to see. In the lab's Exercise 4, the tiny
GPT trained with **no** position signal reaches a validation loss of about 1.59, against 1.544 with
learned positions, and shuffling its context hurts it just as much. Haviv et al. (2022) found the same
in much larger language models. Position signals still help, and real decoders use them; "blind to
order without them" is a statement about attention without a causal mask.

## Pretraining and the LLM Families

Does position help on a real task? The lab trains a two-block Transformer encoder on L21's 25,000 IMDB
reviews, once without and once with positional encoding:

| Model (IMDB, 10,000 test reviews) | Test accuracy |
|---|---:|
| Bag of embeddings (L21) | 0.8662 |
| Self-attention + attention pooling (L21) | 0.8514 |
| Transformer encoder, no positional encoding | 0.8483 |
| Transformer encoder, sinusoidal positional encoding | 0.8483 |

Under these conditions (a small model, trained from scratch for 5 epochs on 25,000 labeled reviews),
position adds nothing to accuracy: with other seeds and on other machines, the version with positions
scored the same or lower (by up to about 0.016), never higher. That is a result about this setup, not
proof that word order is useless for sentiment. L21's same-word pairs now get different scores, so the
model *can* tell the orders apart, but it has not learned what the order means: over eight such pairs,
the more positive sentence scored higher in 6 (anywhere from 2 to 7 in our runs with other seeds), the
differences are mostly tiny, and "this movie is not bad, it is good" is still called negative (the
pairs are short, made-up sentences, so read them with care; the lab's Step 7 shows how fragile they are).

The likely reason is the training signal. A review's label depends mostly on which words it contains,
and each review, about 230 words long on average, gives the model a single label to learn from. The
tiny GPT gets a target at every character, and its objective cannot be met without order: shuffle its
context and its loss jumps. **Positional encoding makes order available; the training objective decides
whether the model uses it.**

That is why modern models are **pretrained**: first on enormous amounts of unlabeled text, with an
objective that cannot be met without word order, then adapted to the task.

- **BERT** (Devlin et al., 2019): encoder-only, no causal mask. Pretrained by hiding about 15% of the
  words (replacing them with a `[MASK]` token, a different "mask" from the attention masks) and
  predicting them from both sides (masked language modeling). Then **fine-tuned** with a small task
  head: classification, tagging, retrieval. Good at *understanding* a whole input.
- **GPT** (Radford et al., 2018 onward): decoder-only, causal mask. Pretrained on next-token prediction,
  exactly the lab's tiny GPT at a vastly larger scale. Good at *generating*; chat models are GPT-style
  models tuned further to follow instructions.

The block has also been refined since 2017. A GPT-style model today typically differs from the 2017
paper in these parts:

| Part | 2017 Transformer | Typical current LLM |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | encoder-decoder | decoder-only |
| Norm position | Post-LN | Pre-LN |
| Normalization | layer norm | RMSNorm (scale only, no mean subtraction) |
| Positions | sinusoidal, added | learned (GPT-2/3), then rotary (RoPE) |
| FFN activation | ReLU | GELU, then SwiGLU |

The idea is unchanged: attention to mix positions, a feed-forward network to transform them, residual
connections and normalization to stack them, a position signal for order, and a mask to decide who sees
whom.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Thinking positional encoding is optional in an encoder.** Without it, self-attention with no causal
  mask is blind to order: the lab's order task stays at chance, and shuffling the tokens after `CLS`
  does not change the logits. (Moving `CLS` itself would change them: the readout would read another
  token.)
- **Thinking every Transformer is blind to order without it.** A causal decoder is not (see "Does a
  decoder need a position signal?" above).
- **Thinking positional encoding is enough.** It makes order *available*. The model uses it only when
  the training signal needs order, which is likely why IMDB accuracy did not move, and why pretraining
  exists.
- **Reading attention weights as an explanation.** A head that puts 0.97 of its weight on B could be
  removed at no cost in the lab, and the head that mattered most looked mixed on average; switching
  parts off (an ablation) tests what they contribute.
- **Confusing layer norm with batch norm.** Layer norm standardizes each token over its features;
  batch norm (L17) each feature over the batch. Transformers use layer norm.
- **Thinking multi-head means deeper, or free.** Heads are side by side at the same depth (depth comes
  from stacking blocks); their matrix products cost the same as one head's, but the softmax runs $h$
  times, and an implementation that stores the weights needs $h$ times the memory.
- **Dropping the residual in a deep stack.** Without it, the lab's 6-block model never learned.
- **Training a decoder without the causal mask.** The loss looks excellent because the model copies
  the answer; generation then fails completely.
- **Thinking one block is the model.** A Transformer is an embedding, a position signal, a stack of
  blocks, and a task head.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is this really what GPT and BERT are?"** -- The block is. Real models are much bigger (BERT-base: 12
blocks, $d = 768$, 12 heads, 110 million parameters; GPT-3: 96 blocks, $d = 12{,}288$, 96 heads, 175
billion), read **subword** tokens rather than characters or whole words, are pretrained on huge text
collections, and use the refined parts in the table above. The mechanism is the one in the lab.

**"Why both attention and a feed-forward network?"** -- They do different jobs. Attention **mixes**
information across positions but is, per position, just a weighted average of value vectors; the FFN
**transforms** each position with a nonlinearity. Alternating them (mix, transform, mix, transform) is
what gives the stack its power. The FFN also holds a large share of each block's parameters: about half in the lab's block, about two-thirds at the usual 4-times width.

**"Why did the 2017 model need a learning-rate warm-up?"** -- In a Post-LN stack, every path from the
output back to the early layers passes through a layer norm per sublayer, and at the start of training
the gradients near the top can be large. Full-size steps from the first update can push the model into a
state it never leaves (the lab's 12-block model). Starting with tiny steps and growing them (the 2017
paper warmed up over 4,000 steps) avoids that. Pre-LN keeps an unnormalized residual path from top to
bottom and depends much less on a warm-up (Xiong et al., 2020): the lab's 12-block Pre-LN model needs
none. Most models since GPT-2 are Pre-LN, and large ones still use a warm-up (GPT-3 did, for example),
as one more safeguard at a scale where a failed run is very expensive.

**"Do Transformers only do language?"** -- No. Vision Transformers cut an image into patches and treat
them as tokens (L20 mentioned the masked autoencoder that trains one), and the same block handles
audio, protein sequences and more: anything that can be written as a sequence of tokens.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| Multi-head attention | `h` heads, each projecting the whole token to `d/h` numbers; concatenated, mixed by `Wo` |
| Cost of heads | same matrix products as one head; `h` softmaxes; `h` times the weight memory if stored |
| Attention weights | where a head looks, not what the answer needs: test with an ablation |
| Positional encoding | sinusoidal or learned vectors added to the tokens; rotary rotates Q and K in every layer |
| Layer norm | standardize each token over its own features; independent of the batch |
| Encoder block | self-attention + FFN, each wrapped in residual + layer norm; shape in = shape out |
| Post-LN vs Pre-LN | `LN(x+f(x))` (2017, needs warm-up when deep) vs `x+f(LN(x))` (GPT-2 on, final norm) |
| Causal mask | `-inf` above the diagonal: each position sees only its past |
| Next-token training | targets = inputs shifted by one; every position of a window is an example |
| Generation | last position's scores, sample, append, repeat; crop to the context window |
| Temperature | divide the scores before the softmax: below 1 sharper, above 1 flatter |
| BERT vs GPT | encoder-only, masked words, understanding vs decoder-only, next token, generation |
| Position and order | an encoder needs it; a causal decoder can learn order without it |
| Position is not enough | it makes order available; the training objective must need it |

## Where to Go Deeper

- **Course text:** Géron, *Hands-On Machine Learning*, ch. 16 -- the Transformer (multi-head attention,
  positional encoding, encoder and decoder) with worked code.
- **Foundational:** Vaswani et al. (2017), *Attention Is All You Need* -- the paper; after the lab it reads
  as a description of what you built.
- **Visual:** Jay Alammar, *The Illustrated Transformer* -- the architecture picture by picture, from one
  head to the full encoder-decoder.
- **Norm placement:** Xiong et al. (2020), *On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture* --
  why Post-LN needs a warm-up and Pre-LN depends on it much less.
- **Rotary positions:** Su et al. (2021), *RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position
  Embedding*.
- **Decoders without positions:** Haviv et al. (2022), *Transformer Language Models without Positional
  Encodings Still Learn Positional Information*.
- **The two families:** Devlin et al. (2019), *BERT*; Radford et al. (2019), *Language Models are
  Unsupervised Multitask Learners* (GPT-2).
- **Data:** Maas et al. (2011), *Learning Word Vectors for Sentiment Analysis* -- the IMDB review
  dataset.
